title: Length-aware KV + Scheduler Playbook
content:
Purpose and scope:

This is a practical playbook for handling variable sequence length workloads in the runtime with a focus on three coordinated subsystems: the scheduler, kernel selection, and the KV cache. It consolidates operational heuristics and small design experiments we want to try before formalizing as an RFC. The goal is to reduce wasted compute from padding while keeping tail latency predictable and preserving KV cache hit rates for multi-turn chat.

Problem statement (brief):

- Real workloads are heavy-tailed by sequence length. Naive batching with global padding causes significant wasted token compute and raises per-token cost.
- Aggressive bucketing reduces padding waste but fragments batches, lowering throughput and increasing kernel kernel-launch overheads and tail latencies.
- KV cache sensitivity: caches are keyed by (request id, model version, sequence prefix). When we pack sequences or fragment execution, cache reuse can be diminished (stale or partial KV entries).

Design goals (practical):

1) Minimize total padded tokens across the fleet (cost) without violating SLOs for p99 latency.
2) Keep kernel warm paths (fewer model-variant launches) and avoid excessive kernel switching.
3) Preserve KV cache hit probability for sessioned interactive traffic.

High-level approach (summary):

Introduce a length-aware scheduling tier that performs lightweight per-request profiling at enqueue time, then places requests into one of three cooperative flow lanes: short, medium, and long. Each lane uses a different packing and kernel strategy and coordinates with a shared KV cache policy that is lane-aware (hot prefixes pinned to short lane, longer prefixes allowed to migrate).

Key ideas and terminology:

- micro-buckets: small, time-windowed bins (e.g., 5–15ms accumulation) within each lane. Micro-buckets enforce an upper pad cap so no request ever gets padded above lane_max_length.

- progressive kernel narrowing: start execution on a generic kernel that supports multiple sequence sizes efficiently (low startup cost). If a micro-bucket reaches high occupancy and sequences align, switch (upgrade) that micro-bucket to a specialized high-throughput kernel for that size range. Downgrade when occupancy drops for N consecutive windows.

- session affinity for KV: requests with an active session id carry a soft affinity tag so their KV entries are preferentially kept in the lane that most frequently serves their sequence lengths. When migrating lanes due to length growth, mark KV entries as migratory to avoid immediate eviction.

- merge-on-evict padding (MOE): when eviction is necessary in the KV cache due to memory pressure, prefer to evict entries whose prefixes are short and have low reuse probability; long prefixes with recent hits are promoted. This keeps long-session conversational KV contents available.

Scheduler details (operational):

1) Enqueue profiling: cheap estimator computes input_length_tokens, estimated_completion_tokens (from user hints or historical predicates), and session_tag. It returns lane = f(input_length_tokens, est_completion). Default thresholds: short < 64, medium 64–512, long >512. These thresholds are tunable per model family.

2) Micro-bucket policy: each lane has micro-buckets that accumulate for a max wait time (latency cap) or until item count reaches N. Micro-buckets track max_length seen; a pad cap equals min(max_length, lane_max_length). When a micro-bucket is sealed for execution, scheduler picks a kernel based on occupancy distribution and sequence-length histogram.

3) Adaptive wait: short lane implements stricter latency (max wait 6ms) but smaller N; medium tolerates slightly more wait to form efficient packs. Long lane favors single-request early execution unless there is high concurrency of similar long requests.

Kernel selection heuristics:

- Kernel flavors: generic (small startup, supports variable lengths), narrow-optimized (best throughput for a narrow length range), long-stream (optimized for long decode with streaming-friendly KV access).

- Decision signal: micro-bucket occupancy, length variance (stddev), and frequency of specialized-kernel hits historically for that micro-bucket tag. If occupancy > TH_high and stddev < TH_low, choose narrow-optimized. If occupancy low or high variance, choose generic. Long lanes default to long-stream kernel unless contiguous windows suggest narrow lengths.

- Upgrade/downgrade: switching kernel for a slot should be amortized across many batches. Use a cooldown window (e.g., 500ms) before switching back to avoid flip-flopping. Maintain per-instance counters to avoid thrash.

KV cache coordination:

- Lane-aware KV namespaces: the cache stores entries with an additional lane_tag. Eviction and pinning honor lane priorities: short lane pinned entries are small but hot (token prefixes in completions), long lane entries are larger and pinned only if recent hits > K.

- Partial reuse policy: allow reuse of KV prefixes even when the incoming batch includes packed shorter sequences. Implement a policy to fetch prefix slices without reconstructing full KV objects (requires KV entries to be addressable by prefix-length).

- Write consistency and migration: when a request grows (e.g., short->medium), mark the KV entry as migrating for M seconds; servicing nodes can fetch from origin store or accept stale until new prefix is populated. This reduces eviction churn when users switch modes mid-conversation.

Safety, observability and metrics to add:

- New per-lane metrics: micro-bucket pad_waste_tokens, kernel-switch-rate, kernel-utilization, kv-hit-by-lane, kv-eviction-reason.
- Latency SLO sub-guardrails: p50/p95/p99 per-lane and per-kernel. Alert on kernel-switch-rate spikes.
- Cost accounting: compute padded_token_cost and effective_tokens_served to show the cost delta between lanes and kernel choices.

Operational experiments (A/B candidates):

1) Baseline vs. lane-aware: deploy lane-aware scheduler on a small fraction of serving fleet and compare padded-token-savings and p99 latency.
2) Progressive kernel narrowing: run trial where a subset of instances allow kernel upgrades; measure throughput uplift and switch overhead.
3) KV migratory semantics: enable migration tagging for 5% of sessions and measure kv-hit retention and eviction churn.

Open questions and risks:

- Complexity vs. value: adding lane-awareness and kernel-upgrades increases runtime complexity and debugging surface. Need clear rollback gates and feature flags.
- Consistency semantics of migratory KV: potential for stale reads in chat—must align with product-level expectations (does a short delay in new prefix presence affect correctness?).
- Memory fragmentation from lane-isolated KV namespaces: monitor and unify if fragmentation causes underutilization.

Next steps (near-term):

- Prototype micro-buckets + simple lane routing in a staging cluster; collect metrics for pad_waste and p99 before moving to kernel-policy changes.
- Small-scale kernel-upgrade experiment with a narrow-optimized kernel for tokens 64–128 on low-traffic instances.
- Implement lightweight KV prefix addressing to enable partial reuse without full object reconstruction.

Notes to reviewers:

- This is a tactical, implementation-oriented playbook rather than a prescriptive RFC. Please comment with concrete metrics you want to see for each experiment so we can bake them into the rollout plan (e.g., target >20% padded-token reduction with <5% p99 increase).

References and links:

- See CON-8142 for historical bucket experiments and GH-PR-2124 for the earliest kernel hot-swap impl prototype.
